extracted.intended_audience: English-speaking readers and students of Persian literature, translators, and comparative-literature readers
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying stylistic norms, rhetorical conventions, and moral purposes in Persian fables, apologues, letters, and preambles as described in an English translation and commentary. Emphasizes distinctions between florid ornamental prose and clear/simple narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Florid style (Ibâret-e-Rengeen) / Florid diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Persians, in the luxuriance of their imaginations, have embellished wonderfully the less artificial writings of the Hindus; the Ibâret-e-Rengeen, or Florid Style, permits the lowest animal in a fable to 'speak a language which would do honour to a king.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This style is characterized by lavish metaphors, embellished imagery, and elevated speech even for humble subjects (example: the 'Two Cats' fable). The translator notes this as a national tendency in many compositions; literal translations of such florid passages are given. Use this style in works meant to delight by ornament; be aware contemporaneous poets and historians may prefer simpler expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deebâchehs / Flowery introductions allow rhetorical latitude
rubrics_metrics.description: In the deebâchehs, or introductions to letters or books, 'the fiery steed of the two-tongued pen' is allowed to run wild amidst a rich pasture of imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preambles commonly employ extravagant hyperbole, extended praise of saints and princes, and luxuriant metaphor (illustrated by the literal translation of a Persian treaty preamble). Such introductions can be highly ornate and conventional; authors may use them to display rhetorical skill or to secure dignity for the parties named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowery preambles to treaties (hyperbolical praise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaty preambles often open with extended praise: 'After the voice is raised to the praise and glory of the God of the world,' followed by extravagant epithets for sovereigns and angels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hyperbole serves diplomatic function—saving the dignity of the Persian king while also allowing courteous mention of the foreign sovereign (e.g., limiting English rule 'to an undisputed sovereignty of the seas'). Writers use florid language to avoid offense and to balance claims of superiority. When composing diplomatic preambles, employ abundant epithets but craft them to preserve relative dignity between parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and plain narration (exemplars: Firdousee, Nizâmee, Sâdee, Anwerree)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many exceptions to the redundant style; in the pages of their greatest poets we meet 'many passages as remarkable for the beauty and simplicity of the expression, as the truth and elevation of the sentiments,' and some historians give 'plain narrations of facts, unencumbered with those ornaments and metaphors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For histories and serious narrative, prefer clear, unornamented prose that conveys facts directly. This style is judged superior for truth, elevation, and the faithful recounting of events; translators and writers should emulate the 'clear and nervous' prose when accuracy and force are desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apologues and fables as vehicles for moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Persian apologues and fables (e.g., the 'Two Cats') employ personified animals and rich metaphor to teach moral lessons—contentment, the dangers of covetousness, and the value of moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose fables where even lowly creatures speak in lofty terms; center a single moral (e.g., 'Content, with the most frugal fare, is preferable'). Use vivid scenes and an instructive ending. The translator includes poetical verses and common proverbial remarks as part of the apologue tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral theme: contentment over covetousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables often dramatize that 'contentment makes men rich' and that covetous ambition leads to disappointment and death (illustrated by the fate of the old woman's cat and the sultan's feasts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize contrasts between modest, contented life and the hazards of sudden ambition; use concrete episodic outcomes (e.g., death by arrow) to moralize. The narrator explicitly frames such apologues as exemplifying this moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persian letter style: 'clear and nervous' when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Persian letters are written 'in a style at once clear and nervous' and convey official duties and conceptions (e.g., the letter of Nizâm-ool-Mulk to Mahomed Shâh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting instructive or political letters, aim for direct, forceful language that communicates duties and counsel plainly rather than relying on ornate metaphor. The Nizâm-ool-Mulk letter is given as a model for transmitting ideas about governance concisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of princes (as counselled by Nizâm-ool-Mulk)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duties of princes include: ensuring laws are strictly obeyed; preserving the honour of subjects; rendering justice to all; distinguishing and rewarding loyal nobles; seeking wholesome pleasures in woods and deserts; chastising the seditious; watching over rights and happiness of lower orders; shunning the mean and abstaining from prohibited practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items constitute the expected moral and political responsibilities of a 'good and great monarch' in Persian political thought. When composing didactic political letters or counsel, enumerate such duties and connect them to restoring ancient splendour and virtuous rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military and expansion duties of princes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of princes 'to be constantly employed in enlarging their dominions, and in encouraging and rewarding their soldiery; it being in the seat of his saddle alone that a king can properly repose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal monarch is martial and expansionist; authors advising rulers should stress active military leadership and the cultivation of a soldiery rewarded for service. Cultural ideals (e.g., austere traditions like birthing on the saddle-cloth) are invoked to maintain martial virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial and priestly humility (Shaikh-ool-Islâm example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge should combine 'sense and information with piety and humility.' He may practice self-denial (e.g., returning costly spectacles, declining displays) to preserve public confidence and to act as a check on despotic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray judges and religious ministers as modest, tolerant, and cautious of ostentation; justify acts of apparent rudeness as duty-bound self-restraint. Use anecdotes (Aboo Yûsuph refusing to decide beyond his competence) to model judicial humility and moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance toward Soofees: value virtues despite doctrinal errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Soofees are often held up by Mahomedan priests as objects of execration for their visionary doctrines, many good and exemplary men are included among them; 'even in their wildest wanderings they convey the most important lessons.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing religious or mystical schools, weigh virtues and exemplary conduct alongside doctrinal errors; allow that poetic and ethical insights (e.g., from Hâfiz and Sâdee) merit appreciation. Use balanced criticism rather than blanket condemnation.
